content: The administration of ZDV (zidovudine) therapy is clinically indicated for the health of pregnant women with HIV. The additional risks associated with the ACTG Protocol 076 regimen include the discomfort of another intravenous infusion during labor and the potential effects of an additional six weeks of ZDV exposure on the infant. Recommendation: Healthcare providers should recommend initiating antenatal ZDV therapy for the woman’s health benefit. The intrapartum and neonatal components of the ACTG Protocol 076 regimen should also be recommended until further data becomes available. This recommendation should be presented within the context of a thorough risk-benefit discussion with the pregnant woman. For pregnant women with HIV who have a history of extensive ZDV therapy (greater than six months) or other antiretroviral therapy prior to pregnancy, there are specific considerations. Women with prior extensive ZDV therapy may harbor viral strains with reduced susceptibility to ZDV. These resistant strains of HIV can potentially be transmitted from mother to fetus, although the frequency of such transmission is unknown. Resistance to ZDV tends to emerge more rapidly when therapy is initiated during later stages of HIV disease. The development of ZDV resistance follows a temporal pattern, with the level of resistance proportional to the number of mutations in the reverse transcriptase-coding region of HIV. Phenotypically and genotypically diverse HIV populations can coexist in patients receiving ZDV therapy. Studies have shown that ZDV-resistant strains appear earlier in patients with advanced HIV disease compared to those who begin ZDV therapy in the early stages of the disease. After 12 months of ZDV therapy, viral isolates from 89% of patients with late-stage disease and 31% of those with early-stage disease were resistant. However, only 33% of late-stage patients demonstrated high-level resistance, defined as a 100-fold decrease in susceptibility. Resistance was more likely to be observed in patients with low CD4+ T-lymphocyte counts at the initiation of therapy. For example, one-year estimated resistance rates were 27% for patients with baseline CD4+ counts >400 cells/µL, 41% for those with counts between 100-400 cells/µL, and 89% for those with counts <100 cells/µL. High-level resistance develops after 6-18 months of therapy in advanced disease but is delayed until after 24 months in early-stage disease. Thus, ZDV-resistant strains are more common in women with advanced disease who have undergone prolonged therapy. Resistance may also be more prevalent in individuals receiving alternative antiretroviral agents due to disease progression during ZDV therapy. The association between clinical disease progression during ZDV therapy and the development of ZDV resistance remains controversial, as does the persistence of resistance when therapy is switched to an alternative antiretroviral agent. Some studies suggest that in vitro susceptibility to ZDV correlates with clinical outcomes, indicating that ZDV-resistant isolates are associated with diminished efficacy of ZDV and more rapid clinical progression. However, other studies suggest that disease progression may be more closely linked to the development of syncytia-inducing viral phenotypes rather than ZDV resistance. Switching to alternative antiretroviral therapy has been associated with the reversal of ZDV resistance in some studies, but resistance has also been reported to persist for extended periods after discontinuation of ZDV. The prevalence of ZDV-resistant viral strains in women receiving alternative antiretroviral agents due to disease progression has not been well-defined. The ability of ZDV to reduce HIV transmission may be diminished in mothers with predominant ZDV-resistant strains, particularly those with high-level resistance, although this assumption is not yet supported by data. Further clinical trials are needed to evaluate alternative approaches for such women. Recommendation: Due to insufficient data to extrapolate the potential efficacy of the ACTG Protocol 076 regimen for this population, healthcare providers should consider recommending the regimen on a case-by-case basis after discussing the risks and benefits with the pregnant woman. Consultation with experts in HIV infection may be warranted. The ACTG Protocol 076 regimen should be made available to the woman, although its effectiveness may vary depending on her clinical status. For pregnant HIV-infected women who have not received antepartum antiretroviral therapy and are in labor, data from human studies are insufficient to evaluate the potential effectiveness of ZDV in this situation. Because the mother’s exposure to ZDV would be brief, such therapy is unlikely to affect the level of maternal virus in blood or genital secretions. However, due to the intravenous loading dose and continuous infusion of ZDV during labor, the infant will be born with circulating levels of ZDV similar to those of infants whose mothers received both antenatal and intrapartum ZDV. ZDV may have utility for this group of patients, regardless of whether the pregnancy is at term or preterm, because the presence of systemic levels of ZDV in the infant before or shortly after HIV exposure through contact with the mother’s blood and genital secretions during delivery may help prevent intrapartum transmission.
